I am so proud of the students from Christ the King Jesuit College Preparatory School in Chicago who traveled to Washington, D.C., to advocate for their communities.

They were the first advocacy group to meet with me as Member-Elect, and I was impressed by how prepared and informed they were.

These students came with letters, research, and serious concerns about the impact of AI data centers on their neighborhoods. They spoke about electricity and water use, rising utility costs, and the importance of including residents in decisions that affect their communities.

They also asked me to support H.R. 9442, the Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act.
I want to thank these students for taking the time to come to Washington and speak up. I support their efforts to be heard, and I respect the work they put into making their case.

This is what civic engagement looks like, and I want to see more young people getting involved and standing up for what matters to them.

Thank you, Christ the King Jesuit College Prep. Keep up the great work!

Learn more about H.R. 9442:
https://t.co/foSvgBcjs1

#IL07 #YouthLeadership #CommunityAdvocacy

Nvidia Earnings Preview: Key Points to Watch

Against the backdrop of Jensen Huang’s sudden resignation and uncertainty over the outlook for data-center construction after the U.S. midterm elections, investors are closely watching Nvidia’s upcoming quarterly earnings, focusing on changes in the company’s management and trends in AI infrastructure investment.

The CEO succession has become the biggest variable: Prediction markets have already identified former Nvidia vice president and current Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential external successor. Internal Nvidia candidates include interim CEO Colette Kress and Ian Buck, who heads Nvidia’s AI business. Haas is an appealing outside candidate who could lead Nvidia forward.

U.S. AI data-center construction: Whether the U.S. midterm elections affect data-center construction, customer orders and future AI capital expenditure is an important indicator to watch.

Valuation view: We assign Nvidia a fair value of $250 per share and believe its current share price is undervalued, while also emphasizing the valuation risks arising from rapid changes in the AI industry and management uncertainty. If Nvidia can achieve the performance targets it has set for itself—and it has an excellent track record of delivering on its targets so far—its share price could still reach or even exceed our fair-value estimate of $250 per share.

Final assessment: We expect Nvidia to once again beat expectations and raise guidance. Given that capital-expenditure trends among major cloud-computing companies and enterprise customers remain strong, we look forward to Nvidia once again delivering quarterly results above market expectations and further raising its guidance for future performance. We would be very surprised if Nvidia’s results for this quarter fell short of expectations or if it provided a weak outlook for future performance. (Morningstar report dated November 12.)

One of the first peer reviewed studies of its kind reveals that the largest data centers in the US are putting out as much Carbon emissions as some entire countries!

Researchers analyzed 403 data centers across the country and found that they account for 2% of the country's electricity—more than that of New York City and Los Angeles COMBINED!

Just over half of that electricity is powered by burning fossil fuels.

And keep in mind that the figures in the study likely underestimate data center impacts because researchers could only verify a fraction of the total number of facilities.

Another shocking discovery (no pun intended) occurred when researchers realized they were spending hours on end just to find out the locations and sizes of these data centers. 

> “The fact that we had to go through such an extensive reconstruction process just to understand where the infrastructure is and how large it is tells you something about the lack of transparency itself in the industry,” said Gianluca Guidi, the Harvard scientist who led the research team.

> “Communities shouldn’t need a team of Harvard researchers to analyze satellite images to understand their environmental impact,” he said.

Thanks to under-regulation and  policies (or lack thereof) that allow AI companies to operate under a certain level of secrecy, there is no real public list of data centers to work from.

Strict licensing rules also prohibit researchers and reporters from publishing the addresses, names and owners of these facilities.

This is untenable!

If someone wants to collect information on data center operations, they have to sift through literally millions of documents spread out across national, state and local databases.

And to make things worse, hyper-scalers and data center developers are going to whatever lengths they can to obfuscate the environmental impacts and resource consumption of their projects.

All of this secrecy was at the top of voters' minds this month's recent election.

In 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives, voters chose to limit data center development in their communities.

The American people have spoken, yet the AI industry is continuing to rapidly expand its operations across the country without constraint and with little to no oversight.

And as data center development grows, so will its carbon footprint.

> The average facility in the study had an electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts, whereas upcoming projects, such as Meta’s 5-gigawatt Hyperion campus in Louisiana, will have more than 100 times that capacity. 

This is clearly unsustainable! And it's no surprise why so many Americans are opposed to metastatic expansion of AI datacenters in their backyards!

So if you find yourself defending this administration's policies on AI, or if you find yourself making excuses for the big tech giants, their CEOs and executives who are behind this push to inundate our lives with AI technology, just know that you are part of a very small minority of people who seem to have no concerns about the risks involved, nor the fact that these AI oligarchs and evangelists have literally told us to our faces that their goal is a dystopian future where they rule the world and we have no agency.

article.plain_text:
The assistant, mobile experiences, free access and the question of what “open” means.
A clinical question usually comes with work attached. Once a clinician has checked whether a treatment fits the patient in front of them, there may be a note to write, a coverage request to prepare and a patient who needs to understand what happens next.
That follow-on work is what interests me most as a healthcare AI engineer. An assistant that helps with it has to produce an answer that still holds up after it leaves the chat window, when it has become a sentence in a chart or a paragraph in a letter to an insurer.
OpenEvidence is a good product to study with that in mind. It answers clinical questions with cited sources, and since August 2025 it has moved into the surrounding tasks: it can help draft a visit note and prepare paperwork intended to help a patient obtain treatment. Apple has also announced a research study, conducted with OpenEvidence, in which people can ask questions about their own health. OpenEvidence Visits, Access Intelligence, Apple’s announcement.
So I read the public record to understand what clinicians ask it, what the assistant does with an answer, who can use it for free and how much of it anyone can inspect. I worked from product documents, platform terms and published studies, without hands-on testing. Where I explain the product’s appeal, I am offering an interpretation of those sources.
What clinicians are asking OpenEvidence
A JAMA study examined the platform’s activity from January 2024 through June 2026. Over that period, 952,008 clinicians, including 556,200 physicians, submitted 271 million queries. That is a cumulative count across two and a half years. For a single month, June 2026, the study reported 703,265 monthly active users. The author group included OpenEvidence-affiliated researchers. JAMA study.
Those counts show use at scale. I learned more from what the study says about the kind of question. The researchers used a large language model (LLM) to classify a stratified sample of 38.8 million queries. Treatment and management accounted for 33.1% of that sample, and diagnosis for 13.9%.
 
Two query categories are shown, not an exhaustive breakdown. Source: the JAMA study’s 38.8-million-query sample. Classification was performed by an LLM. Queries are not patients or demonstrated improvements in care.
Diagnostic puzzles dominate many medical-AI demonstrations. This sample describes something more ordinary: substantial use around managing care.
The logs record what was asked and how it was categorized. They cannot tell us why a clinician chose the tool, how often the answers were correct or whether patients benefited. My own reading is that a clinician may already know the diagnosis and still need to resolve a question about the evidence, an exception or whether a treatment applies to this patient. Lowering the effort of investigating that question seems a plausible reason to come back.
The current product also lets a clinician decide how much time to spend on an answer. In its September 2026 release, OpenEvidence described Osler as its fast default, Sackett as a deeper and more interactive search model, and Snow as a longer investigation that produces a structured report. The company gives approximate response times of five seconds, thirty seconds and five minutes, respectively. Model-family announcement.
I like what that choice acknowledges. A question that comes up during a consultation may need a different response from one a clinician can investigate after clinic. Whether each mode meets that need still has to be evaluated.
A fourth model, Darwin, is an application-only research preview and sits outside the free product. Its reported results come up later, with the comparisons.
A small 2025 primary-care study gives one view of how an answer might be used. Four physicians rated OpenEvidence’s responses to five retrospectively selected cases involving common chronic conditions. They rated relevance at 3.75 out of 4, while the mean rating for impact on clinical decision-making was 1.95. The answers largely reinforced existing plans. That suggests a role as an evidence check, although five retrospective cases cannot establish a general benefit. Hurt and colleagues.
If the product’s first job is helping a clinician confirm or question a plan, the next thing to understand is what happens to the answer afterward.
What the assistant does after the answer
OpenEvidence launched Visits in August 2025. Its announcement describes encounter transcription, configurable note templates, evidence incorporated into assessment and plan drafting, and follow-up questions that use patient and visit context. It also describes uploading and querying patient documentation. As described, these capabilities place the assistant inside documentation work. Time saved and patient benefit are separate questions that need measurement. Visits announcement.
Consider a deliberately simplified workflow. A clinician asks a question, receives an evidence summary, then incorporates part of it into a note. Reviewing the final note means separating three things: what the patient reported, what the clinician observed and what the system proposed from the literature. A plausible recommendation should not become, by default, a fact about what happened in the encounter.
That is an engineering boundary I would want preserved in any interface of this kind. Source evidence and encounter evidence need distinct identities even when they appear in the same paragraph. This is my design requirement; I have not observed how OpenEvidence handles it.
Access Intelligence, announced November 11, 2026, moves into the work that follows a decision. OpenEvidence says it covers more than 2,500 patient-support programs, with information updated daily, and supports savings offers, enrollment materials and prior-authorization documents. Prior authorization is the process of seeking a payer’s approval before it will cover certain care. Access Intelligence announcement.
The company also says clinicians had already written more than 500,000 prior-authorization documents on the platform. That figure counts generated paperwork. It cannot tell us how many requests were approved, how many patients obtained treatment or whether staff spent less time correcting submissions.
Those are the measures I would use to judge this stage of the product. For an appeal letter, I want to know whether the factual account matches the chart, whether the cited policy applies and whether the letter addresses the payer’s stated reason for denial. A polished letter is one part of that work.
The product idea is persuasive: keep the evidence close to the tasks that depend on it. It also raises the cost of a mistake. An error in an answer can be caught while reading. An error carried into several downstream documents takes more work to locate and correct.
Features like these raise two practical questions. Who can use them, and how much of the system can anyone outside the company inspect?
Who gets free access, and which parts are open source
OpenEvidence’s headline offer is free access for verified U.S. healthcare professionals. Its model guide says Osler, Sackett and Snow are available to verified clinicians with unlimited usage at no cost. The clinical service is not free to every person who visits the website. OpenEvidence, model guide.
Free access is one property. Visible citations are another: an answer shows its sources, so a reader can follow a claim back to the literature.
Open-source software is a different property again. It gives a user rights to inspect, modify and redistribute code under its license. Public model weights would make trained model parameters available, subject to their own terms. Even a downloadable model would need its surrounding software, data access and operating infrastructure to reproduce a complete clinical service.
Is OpenEvidence open source? Parts of its tooling are public; the clinical system, as far as I could find, is not. Its GitHub organization lists projects such as a Celery health-check utility and repositories for common software libraries. That is useful public code, separate from the clinical answer engine. Its Hugging Face organization showed no public models when I checked for this article. GitHub organization, Celery utility, model listing.
The product’s terms grant a limited license to use the service. Its acceptable-use policy prohibits attempts to discover the underlying source code or algorithms through reverse engineering. The public materials I reviewed did not provide the production model weights, a complete training pipeline or a license to run the clinical service independently. As of the research date, the clinical product is a proprietary hosted service, with some public software around it. Terms, section 3, acceptable-use policy.
 
These categories describe different permissions. The assessment reflects public materials available on November 16, 2026; it is not a numerical openness score.
Access to the evidence is one more category. OpenEvidence has agreements with publishers including NEJM, JAMA, Nature and Cochrane. Those agreements can make otherwise hard-to-reach material useful inside a clinical tool. They do not turn every underlying article into openly licensed material that anyone can redistribute or use to train another model. OpenEvidence’s content partnerships, content-use restrictions.
It is fair to ask how much this matters to someone in clinic. Clinicians need useful answers rather than model weights. A clinician should not need to read source code before finding a tool useful, a proprietary tool can be useful, and open source would not by itself establish that medical answers are safe.
The transparency that matters most for clinical use also does not depend on publishing patient records or a publisher’s archive. A system can disclose how it was evaluated, identify the version in use and show exactly which source supports a claim.
Two mobile experiences for two different audiences
Mobile is where access is easiest to misread, because two separate things are involved.
The first is OpenEvidence’s own clinician app. Its U.S. App Store listing identifies OpenEvidence Inc. as the developer, lists a zero download price and explicitly requires healthcare-professional verification. The listing dates its original release to August 2024. A free download does not change eligibility: the verification requirement applies on the phone too. Official App Store listing.
The second is much newer and belongs to Apple. On November 15, 2026, Apple announced the Apple Health AI Usage Study, conducted with OpenEvidence. It is a U.S. research study with an associated app, intended to examine trust, comprehension, answer quality and people’s engagement with conversational health AI. Participants can ask health questions and see citations. They can also choose to share certain HealthKit data, such as sleep, activity, resting heart rate or lab results. Apple’s study announcement.
 
Shared medical sources do not give clinicians and patients the same context for interpreting an answer. Illustration, not a screenshot of either app.
The announced capacity is up to 200,000 eligible participants, which is a recruitment ceiling and should not be read as an enrollment count. Participants must be at least 21, live in the United States and have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone running iOS 26 or later. Apple also says study data will not be used to train AI models and that sharing HealthKit data and survey responses is under participants’ control.
The change in audience is what makes the research necessary. A clinician may read an answer with a diagnosis, medication list and physical examination in mind. A patient may be trying to work out whether a symptom deserves attention, or what a lab result means. The same reference can be interpreted very differently in those two settings.
For a consumer experience, I would look past whether an answer sounds understandable. I would want to know whether the person understands its uncertainty, whether it helps them prepare a better question for their clinician, and whether it could create false reassurance or unnecessary alarm. Those are my proposed evaluation questions. Apple has announced a study design, so better preparation for a clinical conversation is a possibility the study can test.
How to check a citation before the claim travels
Both audiences are shown citations, and that is one of the most useful things about the product. A visible source gives the reader somewhere to go next.
It also creates a tempting shortcut. A real paper beneath a fluent answer can make the answer feel verified before anyone has checked whether the paper supports it.
A July 2026 pharmacy critique in JACCP supplies a concrete example. The authors examined responses to a question about incomplete miscarriage, including queries made in May and November 2025. They reported that the system relied on studies whose populations excluded the condition asked about. In the later response, it also made conflicting claims using the same source and assigned an efficacy figure to the wrong intervention. Bergsbaken and colleagues, full article.
The critique is illustrative and based on 2025 queries, so it says nothing about the product’s current error rate. Its lasting value is the mechanism it shows. A reference can exist, concern the right broad topic and still fail to support the sentence attached to it. The population, comparison and outcome have to match the question too.
 
An author-designed review process. It does not depict OpenEvidence’s internal architecture.
The two aids below offer a way to make that check routine. Both are my own proposals for manual review. They are not product features, I have not tested them inside OpenEvidence, and they have not been validated to reduce errors.
The first is a follow-up prompt a clinician could adapt after an initial question:

A better-shaped answer can still be wrong, so the next step is to open the consequential source and compare it with the claim. In the published miscarriage example, checking the study’s excluded population would have exposed the mismatch.
The second aid is for a claim that needs to be retained. A compact review record preserves more context than a screenshot of the answer alone:
Question and date: What was asked, and when
Product mode or visible version: Which system produced the answer
Decision-relevant claim: The exact statement being considered
Source and location: The article, guideline section or table
Applicability: Why its population and comparison fit, or do not fit
Reviewer’s conclusion: Supported, unsupported or still unresolved
Intended use: Whether the claim is informational or will enter a note, letter or decision
The record captures the reasoning a future reviewer would need. No model weights are required to notice that a paper excludes the population in the question.
What comparative studies say, and which versions they describe
Checking one claim at a time is slow, so it is natural to want a shortcut: which tool is simply more accurate? The published comparisons help, within their dates.
A Nature Medicine study compared OpenEvidence and UpToDate Expert AI with GPT-5.2, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and Claude Opus 4.6. It included 500 MedQA questions, 500 HealthBench items and 100 de-identified questions collected from clinicians using an LLM in practice. Twelve clinicians performed randomized, blinded reviews of answers to the clinical questions. The general-purpose models performed better on the study’s evaluations. Vishwanath and colleagues.
That result is a reason for caution about choosing a clinical tool on specialist branding alone. Its limits matter just as much. The study accessed OpenEvidence in September 2025 and February 2026, so it cannot settle how the September 2026 model family performs. The researchers did not evaluate citation quality or response latency, and the clinical questions originated in use of a general-purpose model. One author disclosed consulting for Google, among other interests.
OpenEvidence subsequently reported a perfect MedQA score for Darwin and other strong benchmark results. Those are company-reported results for a restricted research model, and they should not be attributed to every answer from Osler, Sackett or Snow. The two sets of results concern different systems, times and evaluation conditions, so neither cancels the other. Darwin announcement.
The question for a clinician today is narrower than any ranking: how does the available version, in the intended workflow, perform on the kinds of questions they need answered?
Teams that want to answer it systematically should arrange authorized access first. OpenEvidence’s acceptable-use policy restricts automated collection and certain systematic querying without authorization, and its research-preview route is distinct from an unrestricted public API. Acceptable-use policy, research-access description.
How free access is paid for, and how the data policies differ
Unlimited use at no cost has to be funded somehow. Advertising helps support OpenEvidence’s free service. Its advertising policies require ads to be identifiable and set rules intended to keep advertising distinct from clinical content. The JACCP critique also discusses advertising as the business model supporting free access. Advertising policies, JACCP critique.
The arrangement lowers the subscription barrier for clinicians, which I count as valuable. It also makes the separation between commercial interests and medical answers consequential. I found policy commitments and no evidence that an advertiser had influenced a particular answer; the existence of ads is no basis for inferring it. A policy is also different from an independent audit.
What a reader or researcher can observe is concrete: whether sponsored placements are unmistakable, whether they can be told apart from evidence, whether alternative treatments and conflicting findings are represented appropriately, and whether researchers can study those questions under a clear access arrangement.
Data use deserves the same precision. OpenEvidence’s privacy policy states that it does not train AI models on protected health information. It separately discusses professional account data, advertising and some research and development uses of aggregated or de-identified information. Each statement has its own scope, and the policy supports neither “it never uses data” nor a claim that it trains on patient records. Privacy policy.
For a healthcare organization, the relevant question is how a specific feature handles the information its staff will submit, under the applicable agreement and local rules. The clinical app’s policy and Apple’s study commitments should be reviewed separately, because they cover different services and different participants.
What I’ll be watching, and one habit to keep
I began with the work attached to a clinical question. OpenEvidence’s appeal, as I read the public record, is that it lowers the effort and subscription cost of reaching medical knowledge, then puts that knowledge beside the note and the paperwork that follow.
The evidence I would most like to see is tied to that same work. Independent evaluations of the current named models would help, since published results apply to specific versions and dates. So would prospective studies of what happens in practice: fewer unsupported claims in final notes, less correction time for clinicians, coverage requests that address the right criteria, and patients who understand their next steps more accurately. Those outcomes would tell me more than another count of generated answers. Results from Apple’s study, when they come, should say something about how people outside the clinic read a cited answer.
The habit is available today, and it needs nothing from the company. When an answer is about to become a note, an appeal or a clinical decision, open the source behind the sentence. Check that its population, comparison and outcome match the question, and that you can explain why it supports the words you are about to use.
Research note: This article reviews public product documents, platform terms, an App Store record and published studies as of November 16, 2026. It is not a hands-on clinical validation of OpenEvidence. Product claims, study findings and my proposed design or review practices are identified separately. Illustrations were created in Midjourney; diagrams and charts were created in Excalidraw using Geist Serif.

Today's priorities: Qwen's new flagship, healthcare computer-use agents, and automatic inference routing.

For a one-person software factory, the question is not how many models you connect. It is whether they complete real work reliably and affordably.

1. Qwen4-Max: test it, don't blend unrelated benchmarks

Alibaba announced Qwen4-Max with a new MoE architecture, native vision, and a 1M-token context window. Reported size: 2.4T total parameters, 71B active per token.

Max is NOT open-weight. Smaller models in the family are planned for release with open weights. Those are different things.

On Alibaba's own Work360 evaluation, average task cost fell from $4.43 to $1.67, with about 35% fewer tokens in High mode. These are vendor-reported results.

Artificial Analysis independently scored it 43 on its Intelligence Index: nine points above Qwen3.8-Max, three below Kimi K3.1 Pro. Different tests and configurations do not establish universal superiority.

My approach: compare repository changes, tool use, regression results, cost, runtime, and rework before changing the default model.

https://t.co/ieukkjssY7
Independent evaluation:
https://t.co/D2qlYqUxLE

2. Healthcare agents: existing software, human approval, audit trails

OpenAI's ChatGPT for Healthcare update adds computer-use agents for existing EHR and insurance portals, enhanced clinical retrieval, and over 20 healthcare plugins.

OpenAI reports that 99% of 325 evaluated tasks were rated clinically safe. This is NOT a claim of zero real-world risk or a substitute for supervision, permissions, and accountability.

Its Academic Researchers program targets 200,000 researchers, with applications for 50,000 Plus grants planned to open November 23. A separate survey of over 1,800 researchers reports large perceived time savings—not causal proof of productivity gains.

OpenAI also announced embedded assessments with Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire.

The reusable pattern: let agents operate existing systems, require approval for consequential actions, and retain execution records.

3. Hugging Face × OpenRouter: easier routing, a migration caveat

The partnership routes language-model requests by price, speed, and reliability, with automatic failover. Existing HF tokens and code remain usable; image, audio, and video generation stay with HF.

But language-model calls no longer support custom provider keys. If your stack depends on those, check migration requirements and timing rather than assuming a seamless upgrade.

Routing is useful only if a provider failure doesn't stop delivery—and the fallback still passes your tests.

https://t.co/738xy2lXjq

4. Perplexity: distinguish research commitments from delivered results

Frontier Research plans at least 10,000 GPUs for multi-agent orchestration, continual learning, and automated researchers, with promises of evaluations, papers, and open models and tools. Watch what becomes reproducible and usable.

https://t.co/1X659h7y0w

5. From tasks to goals

Harrison Chase's argument has practical implications: define triggers, progress evidence, approval points, and stop conditions—not just a broad instruction to improve a product.

https://t.co/Of4QgSSFjp

Bottom line: cheaper models are a starting point. Reliable execution, tested fallbacks, and verifiable results are what make a one-person software factory efficient.

$MU reported fiscal 2026 revenue of $133.188bn, compared with $37.378bn in fiscal 2025. That is approximately 3.56x in one year. The surprising part is not simply the volume of AI memory demand. It is the margin expansion: reported gross margin increased from 39.8% to 80.7%, a gain of 40.9 percentage points.

That changes the earnings sensitivity dramatically. At $133.188bn of sales, each one percentage point of gross margin represents roughly $1.332bn of annual gross profit, before tax and other costs. If the margin were to fall by five points on an unchanged revenue base, the annual gross-profit impact would be about $6.66bn. This is why a seemingly small change in HBM pricing, yield, mix or DRAM supply can have an outsized effect on valuation.

The company reported fiscal 2026 net capex of $27.37bn and adjusted free cash flow of $62.31bn. That is strong cash conversion, but it must be tested through the next supply cycle. Memory has historically been cyclical. AI infrastructure demand can improve the structural mix without eliminating capacity-driven price declines. The economic pathway is HBM and server memory scarcity leading to higher pricing and richer mix, then higher gross profit and cash generation. The reversal pathway is added capacity, competing supply and slower customer deployment.

Micron guided fiscal Q1 2027 revenue to $61.5bn plus or minus $1.5bn. Compared with fiscal Q4 revenue of $54.229bn, the midpoint implies about 13.4% sequential growth. This is guidance rather than achieved sales. The next important evidence is actual realized pricing and margins, not social-media estimates of wafer shortages.

Invalidation would be an unexpected drop in gross margin, inventory build ahead of demand or capex growth that stops translating into cash. A fast-growing earnings stream can still be overvalued. Without a verified latest share price and normalized cycle multiple, I am treating this as a fundamental watch rather than a fresh entry.

$AMD reported Q3 2026 revenue of $13.377bn, but the more useful number is the $8.5bn Data Center segment. That segment was up 97% from $4.3bn a year earlier. It now represents about 63.5% of company revenue. The shift matters because the valuation debate is no longer about whether AMD can sell more server chips. It is about whether that mix can keep pushing operating income higher without an equal rise in operating expenses.

The math is revealing. Consolidated revenue grew 45%, while GAAP operating income rose from $1.270bn to $2.832bn, a 123% increase. That is roughly $1.562bn of incremental operating profit on $4.131bn of incremental sales, or a 37.8% incremental operating margin. This is a more useful indicator of monetization than a GPU shipment headline alone. It does not mean every incremental AI dollar carries that margin: segment mix, R&D timing and other business lines all contribute.

The causal chain is clear: hyperscaler AI and CPU deployment leads to accelerator and EPYC demand, which drives higher data-center revenue, then potential operating leverage. The test is whether the company sustains this contribution as the MI450 and next platform ramp continues. AMD's reported Data Center operating income was $2.9bn, versus $1.1bn a year earlier, but there is no guarantee that this growth repeats as competition and manufacturing costs change.

A $17bn Q4 revenue outlook implies about 27.1% sequential growth from Q3. Investors should ask what share is recognized shipments rather than forward commitments, and whether gross margin holds near guidance as systems scale. The next earnings print must show actual conversion, not simply announcements.

Invalidation: a weaker data-center mix, gross-margin deterioration, or growth that requires materially more spending than expected. I would not call an entry without a verified current price, valuation and chart level. The fundamental inflection is real; the trade setup is not yet proven.

Follow 9-5 Traders for the next evidence-based update when shipment growth becomes reported earnings.

A blue wave swept Democrats into power in Congress and many fast-growing data center states, including Georgia, which will soon have a governor who campaigned on pausing development. Investors, meanwhile, seem anxious about companies tied to AI and the debt-fueled data center build-out.

For ongoing projects that are under construction or have their zoning in order, not much is likely to change.

Chris Clark, CEO of the Georgia Chamber of Commerce, said unplugging projects that are already underway would send an anti-business message that’s antithetical to the way the Peach State has operated for decades under both parties’ rule.

A Democratic-controlled Congress will have the ability to apply additional scrutiny to Big Tech firms and implement new regulations, which some AI executives said they would welcome. Nearly 70% of Georgia voters said they also think AI needs more government regulation, according to an Atlanta Journal-Constitution poll from October.

The data center industry said it will not support a statewide moratorium, setting the stage for legal battles. Newly elected Democrats in other states with lots of data center activity, such as Texas, will have similar debates.
